extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators and practitioners (district courts, Federal Circuit, PTAB/IPR practitioners)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for when and how courts should construe patent claim terms post-O2 Micro, including timing, waiver, factual vs legal dispute framing, and application across Article III and Article I tribunals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction is a matter of law for the court (Markman)
rubrics_metrics.description: In a case tried to a jury, the court has the power and obligation to construe as a matter of law the meaning of language used in the patent claim; construction of a patent claim is a matter of law exclusively for the court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Markman v. Westview Instruments and the Supreme Court affirmance: courts, not juries, interpret the legal meaning of claim language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give words their ordinary and customary meaning (Phillips)
rubrics_metrics.description: The words of a claim 'are generally given their ordinary and customary meaning,' i.e., the meaning a term would have to a person of ordinary skill in the art after reviewing the intrinsic record at the time of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In many cases ordinary meaning is readily apparent; in others, terms with a particular meaning in the art require examination of intrinsic evidence (specification, prosecution history).

rubrics_metrics.name: O2 Micro rule — court must resolve actual disputes about claim scope
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘When the parties raise an actual dispute regarding the proper scope of these claims, the court, not the jury, must resolve that dispute.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If parties present a dispute as to meaning or whether a term allows exceptions, the ordinary meaning may not resolve it and the court must determine claim scope for use in infringement determination.

rubrics_metrics.name: A determination that a term 'needs no construction' may be inadequate
rubrics_metrics.description: A determination that a claim term 'needs no construction' or has the 'plain and ordinary meaning' may be inadequate when a term has more than one 'ordinary' meaning or when reliance on a term's 'ordinary' meaning does not resolve the parties' dispute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts should avoid simply leaving ambiguous or multi-meaning terms to the jury; if the ordinary meaning doesn't resolve the dispute, perform claim construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court not required to construe every limitation
rubrics_metrics.description: District courts are not (and should not be) required to construe every limitation present in a patent's asserted claims; claim construction is a matter of resolution of disputed meanings and technical scope to clarify what the patentee covered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve construction for limitations that are actually disputed or necessary to clarify scope for the factfinder; avoid unnecessary constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not construe when dispute is factual application rather than legal scope
rubrics_metrics.description: If the parties merely have a factual—not legal—dispute as to a claim term (e.g., whether accused products fall within a construed meaning or whether prior art meets a limitation), that is for the jury (or factfinder) and not for claim construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame disputes appropriately: factual disputes about application should be presented as such to avoid O2 Micro invocation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plain and ordinary meaning acceptable when no dispute as to scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts are not required to construe terms beyond their plain and ordinary meaning if there is no dispute as to scope or if a narrower proposed construction is rejected in favor of plain and ordinary meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: when experts' testimony shows the term was not fundamentally in dispute; when proposed constructions improperly read limitations into the claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Over-reliance on 'plain and ordinary meaning' can be litigation misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: A party's blanket reliance on plain and ordinary meaning for all claim terms and failure to engage in the claim construction process in good faith can support a finding of litigation misconduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure parties meaningfully participate in claim construction and do not submit incomplete or misleading extrinsic evidence while claiming no construction is necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courts must resolve disputes even if specification defines the term or parties agree
rubrics_metrics.description: The court is not absolved of its duty to construe actually disputed terms just because the specification defines the term or the parties agree to a construction; the court must give that construction to the jury in its instructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even stipulated constructions or specification-based definitions should be presented as legal instructions to the jury where dispute exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: O2 Micro applies at various stages and forums (motions, pleadings, PTAB, IPRs, reexams)
rubrics_metrics.description: O2 Micro's duty to resolve actual disputes regarding claim scope applies at the motion to dismiss stage, in Article I tribunals (PTAB/IPRs), and in ex parte reexamination contexts—not only at Markman hearings or Article III final judgments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners should consider claim-construction disputes early, as they may be outcome-determinative at pleading or administrative stages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Waiver if O2 Micro challenges not timely brought
rubrics_metrics.description: O2 Micro challenges are waived if not timely brought—parties cannot create a new claim construction dispute after close of the jury trial or on appeal if they failed to present proposed constructions at or prior to trial/Markman.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Raise construction positions at Markman or otherwise clearly and timely in pretrial proceedings; late-first-time appeals of constructions are routinely rejected as waived.

rubrics_metrics.name: Waiver exceptions: preserved by raising at Markman or timely during trial
rubrics_metrics.description: A party preserves O2 Micro issues if it raised the concern in Markman briefing/hearing or brought the dispute to the district court's attention during trial in a timely manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a party argued a construction at Markman and lost, it generally need not reassert it at every subsequent stage to preserve for appeal; raising during trial can also preserve the issue if the court hears arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mid-trial constructions are permissible but must avoid surprise and prejudice
rubrics_metrics.description: A mid-trial adjustment or further construction can be acceptable where a dispute arises, provided it is done early enough to give the parties opportunity to adjust and the district court prevents gamesmanship and unfair advantage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: District courts should solicit input from parties before altering constructions; making further construction without party input is improper (TNS Media).

rubrics_metrics.name: Appellate remedies for O2 Micro errors vary based on prejudice and record
rubrics_metrics.description: If a district court fails to resolve an actual claim-scope dispute, remedies range from vacatur and remand for new proceedings to reversal of the verdict; remand is not always required if the error is harmless and the verdict is supported under the proper construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether to remand depends on whether the jury could have reasonably applied the proper construction and whether prejudice resulted from the court's failure to construe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courts should not convert fundamentally factual questions into legal ones without guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: The Federal Circuit (through dissents) has warned against stretching O2 Micro to convert fundamentally factual jury questions into legal issues for the court without clear standards for what constitutes an 'actual dispute.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious in invoking O2 Micro for simple factual disputes; courts and advocates should seek clarity on what qualifies as an 'actual dispute.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategic framing: present disputes as legal or factual depending on desired outcome
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners should frame their arguments to the court in the light that best advances their position: to obtain a court construction under O2 Micro, argue the matter is a legal dispute of claim meaning/scope; to keep an issue for the jury, emphasize it is factual application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Careful advocacy can determine whether an issue is decided by judge (claim construction) or jury (application). Avoid over-reliance on 'no construction' positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know the O2 Micro landscape and judicial variability
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners should be aware of varying Federal Circuit viewpoints—some judges are more reluctant to find claim-scope disputes—and account for differing approaches when arguing disputes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate that some judges (per dissents) may treat expert disagreements over 'plain and ordinary meaning' as factual and resist converting them into legal disputes; tailor arguments accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bring claim construction disputes to the court's attention as soon as they crystallize
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid waiver by remaining cognizant of claim construction disputes from the outset; raise them at Markman stage ideally, but if they crystallize later bring them to the court promptly, even if trial has begun.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timely identification and presentation reduces risk of waiver and makes it likelier the court will resolve the dispute rather than leave it to the jury.
